title: In what sense the Protestants deny free choice for moral good
source_text: XLIII. Quod si quis quaerat An homo in statu naturae lapsae, sine gratia, sit liber ad bonum morale eligendum, & praecepta Dei servanda? ad hoc negative respondent Protestantes: adeoque eorum plurimi negant post peccatum in homine mansisse liberum arbitrium respectu boni moralis. Non aliud tamen per hoc sibi volunt, quam hominem per suum lapsum factum esse servum & captivum peccati, ejusque arbitrium privatum esse ea libertate quae servituti peccati opponitur: licet in eo manserit libertas illa quae essentialis est agenti intellectuali, & a qua hominis arbitrium absolute consideratum liberum denominatur.
pass_a_gloss: XLIII. But if anyone ask Whether man in the state of fallen nature, without grace, be free for choosing moral good, and for keeping God's precepts? to this the Protestants answer negatively: and so most of them deny that after sin free choice remained in man in respect of moral good. Nothing else however by this do they mean, than that man through his fall has been made the servant and captive of sin, and his choice deprived of that liberty which is opposed to the servitude of sin: although in him there remained that liberty which is essential to an intellectual agent, and from which man's choice absolutely considered is called free.
pass_b_english: Thesis XLIII. If someone asks whether man in the state of fallen nature is free, without grace, to choose moral good and keep God's commandments, the Protestants answer no. So most of them deny that free choice remained in man after sin with regard to moral good.

All they mean by this, though, is that by his fall man became the slave and captive of sin, and his choice lost the freedom that is opposed to the bondage of sin. The freedom essential to an intellectual agent still remained in him, the freedom from which man's choice, considered absolutely, is called free.

lemmas.gloss: to this the Protestants answer negatively
